headline: Local Man Enters Third Day of Mourning After Hour-Long Post Receives Two Likes
subheadline: Friends describe 'hollow' and 'distant' demeanor following Threadit engagement disappointment
summary: A Millbrook resident has been unable to function normally after a post he spent an hour crafting received only two likes, one of which was from his mother.
content:
The post was 847 words long. It represented, according to its author, his "most refined thoughts on the nature of modern existence." It received two likes in 72 hours.

Brian Hollister, 28, has not been the same since.

"He keeps refreshing," reported roommate Sean Chen. "Just sitting there, pulling down on the screen over and over. It's been three days. The number hasn't changed."

The post, shared on Threadit's r/DeepThoughts community, explored themes of digital alienation and the search for meaning in an interconnected world. Hollister spent approximately 65 minutes writing it, 30 minutes editing, and another 20 minutes selecting the perfect time to post based on a guide about optimal engagement windows.

"I thought maybe early evening, when people are winding down," Hollister explained, his voice flat. "I used paragraph breaks. I included a personal anecdote. I did everything right."

The two likes came from his mother, who follows his Threadit account despite repeatedly expressing confusion about how the platform works, and an account that appears to be a bot promoting cryptocurrency.

"His mom's like was immediate," Chen noted. "Like, suspicious immediate. She must have notifications on for his posts. That almost made it worse."

Hollister has since audited his posting history, comparing engagement across different types of content. His findings disturbed him further.

"A picture of my lunch got 47 likes," he said. "It was a sandwich. A mediocre sandwich. But my genuine attempt to connect with humanity through written expression gets two."

Psychologist Dr. Amanda Price recognizes the phenomenon. "We call it 'engagement grief,'" she explained. "Users invest significant emotional and intellectual energy into content, then experience genuine loss when that investment isn't reciprocated. The disconnect between effort and response can feel profoundly isolating."

Hollister attempted to share his feelings about the experience in a follow-up post. It received zero likes.

"Even the bot didn't engage with that one," he noted.

Friends have attempted intervention, offering to like the original post themselves, but Hollister has refused.

"Pity likes are worse than no likes," he insisted. "I'd rather have the hollow nothing than the hollow something."

He has not posted in three days. The Threadit account shows him as "online now" at all hours.

"He's still refreshing," Chen confirmed. "Just in case."
author: Michelle Park, Human Interest
